name: The Teen Idles
label: Dischord
lede: Four Wilson High kids took a Greyhound to California, came home with an X for the back of the hand, and put their $600 into a thousand hand-glued sleeves that became Dischord No. 1.

eras.title: The Cramps did it
eras.text: D.C. punk in early 1979 was a handful of shows and a handful of kids. Two of them went to see The Cramps at the Hall of Nations, and by fall they had a band, though most clubs wouldn't let them in.

years.big: "The first show that made us want to be in a band."
years.h: The Cramps play Georgetown, and two Wilson High kids want in
years.p: [[Ian MacKaye|c12f644b-1066-4ead-b0dd-d0c380f5cca2]] and [[Jeff Nelson|51f7994c-949d-4dbe-89eb-2c33f42a5620]] are in the crowd at the Hall of Nations on February 3. That's Nelson, describing the night to the City Paper.
years.xp: Ian MacKaye later said that until the Cramps show, Ted Nugent was about as wild as music got for him. The Cramps ended that.

years.h: Four Wilson High kids start the Slinkees
years.p: MacKaye plays bass, Nelson drums, [[Geordie Grindle|2f8ebbdb-3b57-4648-a339-bedf27b86ab3]] guitar, and Mark Sullivan sings. They play one show.

years.h: Sullivan leaves for college, and Henry Garfield passes on the mic
years.p: MacKaye's friend Henry Garfield, later [[Henry Rollins|656b39fb-979c-4c57-bb87-61d1a8eb38d1]], can't take the vocal spot, so [[Nathan Strejcek|b53e7b75-696d-43f5-98ff-bc3d104e0d74]] gets it.

years.h: Teen Idles is the new name
years.p: With Strejcek singing, the band drops Slinkees. MacKaye, Nelson, Grindle and Strejcek are the lineup that makes Dischord No. 1.

eras.title: Too young to rock, too loud to stop
eras.text: The Teen Idles lasted about a year and a half, and 1980 was nearly all of it. They chased the Bad Brains, got turned away from clubs for being underage, rode a Greyhound to California, and came back with an idea that outlasted them: an X on the back of the hand.

years.cap: Flyer for Bad Brains, Trenchmouth and the Teen Idles, January 1980
years.h: Turned away at the door while the Bad Brains play
years.p: Many of the Teen Idles and their friends are under 18, and the [[Bad Brains|e919b253-da5b-4aae-a444-6a368376a2d6]] are, in Dischord's words, maybe the greatest band in the world in 1980. Clubs keep showing the kids out.
years.xp: Dischord's band history says the Teen Idles became close friends with the Bad Brains. The age problem pushed them toward pizza parlors, house parties and, eventually, a campaign to get D.C. clubs to let kids in.

years.h: Wherever would have them: pizza parlors, house parties, an art gallery
years.p: Wikipedia says the Teen Idles even land a slot opening for [[Bad Brains|e919b253-da5b-4aae-a444-6a368376a2d6]] at Madam's Organ. The video is a full set at Third Dimensions on July 27.

years.cap: The Teen Idles in California, August 1980
years.h: Greyhound to California, and the X comes home
years.p: The Teen Idles ride west with roadies Mark Sullivan and Henry Garfield, the "fifth Idle." At San Francisco's Mabuhay Gardens, the underage kids get a marker X on their hands so the bar knows not to serve them.
years.xp:
It wasn't a smooth trip. According to Wikipedia, Jeff Nelson spent an hour in police handcuffs soon after they arrived, the Hong Kong Café in Los Angeles turned them away for being underage, and a show opening for the Mentors and Puke, Spit and Guts paid $15. MacKaye recalled that people were freaked out by how fast they played.

Back in D.C., they pitched the Mabuhay system to local clubs: mark the kids, let them in. The 9:30 Club adopted it. MacKaye said the X was meant to signify kids, not straight edge. A few months later an X-marked pair of hands, belonging to his younger brother [[Alec MacKaye|bb05a948-ea44-4c9b-9d19-2a48f757ca22]], was on the cover of Minor Disturbance, and the X came to stand for straight edge anyway.

years.h: Geordie Grindle quits after a long feud with Jeff Nelson
years.p: Per Wikipedia, Grindle's born-again Christian girlfriend disapproved of the band, and friction with atheist Nelson built until he left. That ended the Teen Idles.

years.cap: Flyer for the Teen Idles' final show with SVT, 9:30 Club, November 6, 1980
years.h: Final show at the 9:30 Club, opening for SVT
years.p: The flyer says it plainly: Final Show, Nov. 6th. Too Young to Rock is taped live that night and goes straight onto Minor Disturbance.
years.xp: The flyer bills SVT as coming from San Francisco and already advertises the Minor Disturbance EP at the bottom. The video is the band a week earlier, at the Chancery on Halloween.

q: Let's give it 100 percent, for a minute and a half
years.p: Eight songs, recorded in August 1980 with [[Don Zientara|a495882b-4585-4295-9269-e30c63f279fe]] and [[Skip Groff|8c4d8d50-a6a7-4fa6-9524-6e9c595816c1]]. The Teen Idles' $600 in savings pays for 1,000 copies, sleeves glued by hand, on a label they invent: Dischord.
years.xp:
The eight songs, about nine minutes, were cut at Inner Ear, then a four-track in Zientara's Arlington home. Zientara described the band as them against the world, playing every song as if they'd collapse at the end of it.

Jeff Nelson designed the cover around Susie Josephson's photo of Alec MacKaye's crossed, X-marked hands. The back cover is Jay Rabinowitz's Halloween 1980 photo of the band and friends outside the Chancery.

years.cap: Minor Threat at the Wilson Center, Washington, April 4, 1981: Lyle Preslar, Brian Baker and Ian MacKaye, with Henry Rollins at lower right
years.h: MacKaye picks up the mic, and the Teen Idles become [[Minor Threat|09037f07-42bc-46ac-a1ee-37f834451fee]]
years.p: Ian MacKaye moves from bass to vocals, Jeff Nelson stays on drums, and the new band plays its first show before 1980 is out.

eras.title: What $600 built
eras.text: The band was gone, but Minor Disturbance kept doing its job. Dischord went on releasing its friends' bands one 7-inch at a time, roadie Henry Garfield became Henry Rollins, and the EP stayed in print next to the records it paid for.

years.h: The "fifth Idle" goes west to sing for [[Black Flag|9941a936-196a-4a62-ae53-a69cbc33f20e]]
years.p: Henry Garfield, the roadie on the 1980 California trip, leaves D.C. and fronts Black Flag as Henry Rollins.

years.h: Strejcek runs Dischord for a while, then MacKaye and Nelson take it back
years.p: Former Teen Idles singer Nathan Strejcek takes on the label, but Nelson and MacKaye, unhappy with how little he put in, reclaim it. He goes on to front [[Youth Brigade|7029a4cb-83bc-4e5e-8d94-af9caefc453c]].

years.h: Teen Idles tracks turn up on Flex Your Head
years.p: The compilation is Dischord No. 7, and it serves as a map of early D.C. hardcore.

years.h: Four Old 7"s on a 12" puts Minor Disturbance back in circulation
years.p: With the original pressing long gone, the EP shares an LP with early singles by [[SOA|e54cb250-3502-4c32-9482-70488bd9a8cb]], [[Government Issue|9b952ee8-d45d-4a26-8066-57849d871e06]] and Youth Brigade.

eras.title: Dischord No. 100 goes back to No. 1
eras.text: Fifteen years on, Dischord had outlived nearly every band it started with. When the catalog reached No. 100, the label went back to the Teen Idles, the band behind No. 1.

years.h: Fifteen years after the glued sleeves, Minor Disturbance gets a CD
years.p: The Teen Idles' 1980 EP finally comes out on compact disc.

years.h: Dischord's 100th record is the Teen Idles' 1980 demos
years.p: In February and April 1980 the Teen Idles taped two demo sessions while the engineer and a visiting band laughed at them. Anniversary puts them out sixteen years later.
years.xp: Dischord picked the band behind No. 1 for No. 100, a release meant to celebrate the label's own anniversary. The track titles weren't confirmed, so the card has no song to play.

sources.title: UMD Libraries, Persistent Vision: Teen Idles
